test_text.title: Return of the elm: reintroducing the beloved tree to Britain

article.title: Return of the elm: reintroducing the beloved tree to Britain
glossary: * horticultural analogue: a cultivated plant species that is genetically similar to an existing species

items.sentence_raw: Around 25 million elms, accounting for 90% of all elm trees in the UK, died during the 1960s and '70s of Dutch elm disease.
In the aftermath, the elm, once so dominant in the British landscape, was largely forgotten.
However, there's now hope the elm may be reintroduced to the countryside of central and southern England.
Any reintroduction will start from a very low base.
"The impact of the disease is difficult to picture if you hadn't seen what was there before," says Matt Elliot of the Woodland Trust.
items.explain: Q23: The statement says you understand the disease's effect when you see how common elms once were. The passage says Matt Elliot says you only realise the impact *'when you look at old photographs from the 1960s'* that show elms were everywhere before. Old photographs are the evidence of how prominent elms were. The answer is **A (Matt Elliot)**.

The disease is caused by a fungus that blocks the elms' vascular (water, nutrient and food transport) system, causing branches to wilt and die.
A first epidemic, which occurred in the 1920s, gradually died down, but in the '70s a second epidemic was triggered by shipments of elm from Canada.
items.explain: Q16: The question asks how Dutch elm disease came to Britain. The passage says the 1970s epidemic was *'triggered by shipments of elm from Canada'* — this directly explains how the disease was brought into the country. This detail is in section **B**.

items.sentence_raw: The wood came in the form of logs destined for boat building and its intact bark was perfect for the elm bark beetles that spread the deadly fungus.
This time, the beetles carried a much more virulent strain that destroyed the vast majority of British elms.
Today, elms still exist in the southern English countryside but mostly only in low hedgerows between fields.
"We have millions of small elms in hedgerows but they get targeted by the beetle as soon as they reach a certain size," says Karen Russell, co-author of the report 'Where we are with elm'.
Once the trunk of the elm reaches 10-15 centimetres or so in diameter, it becomes a perfect size for beetles to lay eggs and for the fungus to take hold.
items.explain: Q18: The question asks when young elms become at risk of Dutch elm disease. The passage says *'once the trunk of the elm reaches 10-15 centimetres in diameter, it becomes a perfect size for beetles to lay eggs and the fungus to take hold'*. This describes the exact stage young elms become vulnerable. The answer is **C**.

items.sentence_raw: Yet mature specimens have been identified, in counties such as Cambridgeshire, that are hundreds of years old, and have mysteriously escaped the epidemic.
The key, Russell says, is to identify and study those trees that have survived and work out why they stood tall when millions of others succumbed.
items.explain: Q14: The question talks about research problems from very few surviving large elms. The passage says *'opportunities are limited as the number of these mature survivors is relatively small'* — **'limited opportunities'** are the same as **'research problems'**, and **'mature survivors'** are **'surviving large elms'**. This information is in section **C**.

items.sentence_raw: "What are the reasons for their survival?" asks Russell.
"Avoidance, tolerance, resistance?
We don't know where the balance lies between the three.
I don't see how it can be entirely down to luck."
items.explain: Q21: The statement says there must be a reason some mature elms survived. The passage says Karen Russell says *'I don't see how it can be entirely down to luck'* — **not luck** means there is a real explanation for their survival. The answer is **B (Karen Russell)**.

items.sentence_raw: For centuries, elm ran a close second to oak as the hardwood tree of choice in Britain and was in many instances the most prominent tree in the landscape.
items.explain: Q24: The question says the only tree more popular than elm in Britain for hundreds of years was something. The passage says *'elm ran a close second to oak as the hardwood tree of choice in Britain'* — **'second to oak'** means oak was more popular than elm. The answer is **oak**.

items.sentence_raw: Not only was elm common in European forests, it became a key component of birch, ash and hazel woodlands.
The use of elm is thought to go back to the Bronze Age, when it was widely used for tools.
Elm was also the preferred material for shields and early swords.
In the 18th century, it was planted more widely and its wood was used for items such as storage crates and flooring.
items.explain: Q25: The question says 18th century elm wood was used for boxes and something. The passage says its wood was used for *'storage crates and flooring'* — **'storage crates'** are the same as **'boxes'**. The answer is **flooring**.

items.sentence_raw: It was also suitable for items that experienced high levels of impact and was used to build the keel of the 19th-century sailing ship Cutty Sark as well as mining equipment.
items.explain: Q26: The question says the Cutty Sark's something was built from elm. The passage says elm was used to build the *'keel of the 19th-century sailing ship Cutty Sark'*. This matches the question exactly. The answer is **keel**.

items.sentence_raw: Given how ingrained elm is in British culture, it's unsurprising the tree has many advocates.
Amongst them is Peter Bourne of the National Elm Collection in Brighton.
"I saw Dutch elm disease unfold as a small boy," he says.
"The elm seemed to be part of rural England, but I remember watching trees just lose their leaves and that really stayed with me."
Today, the city of Brighton's elms total about 17,000.
items.explain: Q17: The question describes conditions that let one British location avoid Dutch elm disease. The passage says Brighton's elms survived because *'strong winds from the sea make it difficult for the elm bark beetle to attack'*. **'Brighton'** is the location, and strong sea winds are the special conditions. The answer is **E**.

items.sentence_raw: Local factors appear to have contributed to their survival.
Strong winds from the sea make it difficult for the determined elm bark beetle to attack this coastal city's elm population.
items.explain: Q17: The question describes conditions that let one British location avoid Dutch elm disease. The answer is **E**.

items.sentence_raw: However, the situation is precarious.
"The beetles can just march in if we're not careful, as the threat is right on our doorstep," says Bourne.
items.explain: Q22: The statement says we need to know the disease-carrying insects are very close. The passage says Peter Bourne says *'the threat is right on our doorstep'* — **'right on our doorstep'** means **'not very far away'**. The answer is **C (Peter Bourne)**.

items.sentence_raw: Any prospect of the elm returning relies heavily on trees being either resistant to, or tolerant of, the disease.
This means a widespread reintroduction would involve existing or new hybrid strains derived from resistant, generally non-native elm species.
A new generation of seedlings have been bred and tested to see if they can withstand the fungus by cutting a small slit on the bark and injecting a tiny amount of the pathogen.
"The effects are very quick," says Russell.
items.explain: Q19: The statement says damage from Dutch elm disease becomes visible very fast. The passage says Karen Russell states *'the effects are very quick'*, and you see symptoms in 4 to 6 weeks. **'Effects are very quick'** matches **'damage rapidly becomes visible'**. The answer is **B (Karen Russell)**.

items.sentence_raw: "You return in four to six weeks and trees that are resistant show no symptoms, whereas those that are susceptible show leaf loss and may even have died completely."

items.sentence_raw: All of this raises questions of social acceptance, acknowledges Russell.
"If we're putting elm back into the landscape, a small element of it is not native - are we bothered about that?"
For her, the environmental case for reintroducing elm is strong.
items.explain: Q15: The question refers to different opinions on the value of reintroducing elms. The passage says Russell thinks the environmental case is *'strong'*, but Elliot is *'more wary'* and prefers letting existing elms recover naturally. **Different views on reintroduction** are the core of this section. The answer is **G**.

items.sentence_raw: "They will host wildlife, which is a good thing."

items.sentence_raw: "On the face of it, it seems like a good idea," says Elliot.
The problem, he suggests, is that, "You're replacing a native species with a horticultural analogue*.
You're effectively cloning."
There's also the risk of introducing new diseases.
Rather than plant new elms, the Woodland Trust emphasises providing space to those elms that have survived independently.

items.sentence_raw: "Sometimes the best thing you can do is just give nature time to recover... over time, you might get resistance," says Elliot.
items.explain: Q20: The statement says it may be better to wait for surviving mature elms to grow well on their own. The passage says Matt Elliot says *'sometimes the best thing you can do is just give nature time to recover'*. **'Give nature time to recover'** is the same as **'wait and see'**. The answer is **A (Matt Elliot)**.
